Learning Objectives
Specify the structure and composition of articular cartilage
Explain the catabolic and anabolic components of articular cartilage metabolism
Identify the mechanisms that affect cartilage injury and repair
Overview
Articular cartilage is the smooth, white tissue that covers the bony surfaces of synovial joints1,2
(Figure 1).





It is a specialized hyaline cartilage that lacks a perichondrium and constitutes a firm,
lubricated, and deformable layer between bones that distributes load to minimize friction and
wear.3,4
Articular cartilage thickness is approximately 2 mm, but it varies from joint to joint (ie, from 1
to 7 mm) and decreases with age.2
The biomechanical characteristics of articular cartilage are derived from its unique structure
and components.5
Articular cartilage is composed of mainly extracellular matrix (ECM; 95%) and a sparse
population of chondrocytes (5%).1,2 The major components of the ECM are water, collagen,
and proteoglycans.6
Water makes up 60% to 80% of the wet weight of articular cartilage.3,7
Collagen makes up more than 50% of the dry weight of articular cartilage and 10% to 20% of
the wet weight.2,3
Proteoglycans make up 10% to 15% of the dry weight of articular cartilage.8

Figure 1 Images of articular cartilage. A, Arthroscopic image shows heathy hyaline articular
cartilage from a knee joint. Scale bar: 0.1 cm. B, Gross specimen shows normal cartilage of the
distal femur. C, Histologic image with Safranin O staining shows articular cartilage with matrix
and chondrocytes well organized in each zone. (Courtesy of Aghogho Evuarherhe, Jr, BS,
Chicago IL.)
Structure and Composition of Articular Cartilage
Composition
Chondrocytes
The only cell type found in articular cartilage is the chondrocyte. These cells synthesize and
secrete all the major components of the ECM (collagen, proteoglycans, hyaluronic acid) and
replace degraded matrix molecules to preserve the mechanical properties of cartilage.6,9
Mesenchymal cells aggregate and differentiate into chondroblasts, which ultimately become
chondrocytes.9
Chondrocytes lie within spaces called lacunae and contain a well-developed rough
endoplasmic reticulum (where collagen is synthesized), the Golgi apparatus, glycogen, and
lipids.3,6
In the deeper layers of the cartilage, chondrocytes contain less rough endoplasmic reticulum
and are less metabolically active.9,10
Articular cartilage lacks undifferentiated cells that can migrate and proliferate.7
Water
The most abundant component of articular cartilage is water (60% to 80% of the wet weight).2
Water flow through the articular cartilage is characterized by frictional resistance and
pressurization, which provide the tissue with its biomechanical properties: resistance of high-
compressive joint loads and return to normal shape after deformation (ie, compliance).3-5
Other extracellular fluids in the articular cartilage include dissolved gases, metabolites, and a
large number of cations.7
The exchange of extracellular fluid with synovial fluid ensures that the avascular and aneural
articular cartilage receives oxygen and nutrients.3,7
Collagen

More than 14 types of collagen have been identified.2,7
In the articular cartilage, most of the collagen (90% to 95%) is type II collagen.8,11
A large amount of carbohydrate groups bound to type II collagen attract water into the
intrafibrillar spaces within collagen.8
The triple-helix structure of collagen, which is formed by three alpha chains and is encoded
in the COL2A1 gene, provides important shear and tensile properties that help stabilize the
matrix.10,11
High levels of glycine, proline, hydroxyproline, and hydroxylysine are contained in all collagens
and contribute to the formation of the triple helix8 (Figure 2).
Other ECM collagens include types V, VI, IX, X, and XI.1,2
Type III: increased with normal aging and early tissue repair after injury14,15
Type VI: increased in the early stages of osteoarthritis12,13
Type X: found only near calcified areas of the matrix8
The triple helices of collagens II, IX, and XI line up in a staggered fashion between the
proteoglycan molecules and form cross-linked fibrils that constitute the backbone of the
collagen network.1,2
The cross-linked collagen network and fibrillar organization provide shear and tensile
strength.3,11
The shape of articular cartilage and its material strength also depend on this
organization.5,8

Figure 2 Illustration shows a scheme for the formation of collagen fibrils. The triple helix is made
from three alpha chains forming a procollagen molecule. Outside the cell, the N- and C-terminal
globular domains of the alpha chains are cleaved off to allow fibril formation, which occurs in a
specific quarter-stagger array that ultimately results in the typical banded fibrils seen under
electron microscopy. (Reproduced with permission from Mow VC, Zhu W, Ratcliffe A: Structure
and function of articular cartilage and meniscus, in Mow VC, Hayes WC, eds: Basic Orthopaedic
Biomechanics. New York, NY, Raven Press, 1991, pp 143-198.)
Proteoglycans
Composed of polysaccharides (95%) and proteins (5%)1
Proteoglycans consist of numerous chains of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), or unbranched
polysaccharides made from two disaccharide molecules.2,8
The major GAG chains are chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate.10
GAGs are attached to a protein core via sugar bonds and form a proteoglycan aggrecan
molecule with a bottle-brush appearance1,10 (Figure 3).
Aggrecan molecules bind to hyaluronic acid molecules via link proteins to form a
macromolecule complex known as a proteoglycan aggregate.16
The cross-linked collagen fibrils act as a meshwork that traps proteoglycan aggregates. This
special arrangement of proteoglycans with collagen is called the netting. 7,16

Water-binding properties
Negative charges on the surface of GAGs attract water molecules.8
The hydrophilic nature of proteoglycans causes wet cartilage to swell until restricted by
tension in the collagen network, providing compressive strength in the articular cartilage.3,10
Water is held in place by proteoglycans, which are held by the collagen fibrillar network.2,8
Aggrecans also prevent pathologic degradation of collagen fibrils by collagenases such as
matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-1.8,16
In osteoarthritis, proteoglycan content and keratan sulfate concentration decrease, whereas
proteoglycan degradation and chondroitin 4-sulfate concentration increase.12,13
Keratan sulfate level increases with age, whereas chondroitin 4-sulfate level decreases and
chondroitin 6-sulfate level remains constant.7,14
Other Matrix Molecules
Noncollagenous proteins, such as chondronectin, fibronectin, tenascin, and anchorin, also play
a role in ECM‒chondrocyte interactions.1,2
Minor components (1%): glycoproteins, inorganic salts, cations, gases, lipids, and
phospholipids.1,2
Structure
Articular cartilage has a zonal structure based on the cell morphology and structure of the
ECM.7
This zonal organization helps the tissue withstand shear, compression, and tensile forces.3,5
The articular cartilage consists of four zones, or layers: superficial, middle, deep, and
calcified3,10 (Figure 4 ).
Chondrocyte density decreases progressively with depth of the zones.1

Collagen and water contents also diminish progressively with depth.2,10
Proteoglycan content is lowest in the superficial zone, richer in the middle zone, and maximal
in the deep zone.8,10
Collagen fibrils are oriented parallel to the articular surface in the superficial zone, randomly
in the transitional zone, and perpendicular in the deep zone.7,8
Figure 4 Images show the four zones of articular cartilage. A, Light microscopic image shows
adult human articular cartilage taken from the medial femoral condyle. By definition, the
superficial (S) and transitional (T) zones each constitute 10% of the height of the articular cartilage
layer, the bulk of which (80%) is represented by the radial zone (R). For analytical purposes, the
latter is partitioned into an upper and a lower half, each of which is further subdivided into upper
and lower portions. The layer of calcified cartilage (CC) and the subchondral bone plate
(arrowheads) form relatively thin strata beneath the hyaline articular cartilage tissue. BM = bone

Cartilage 2002;10[7]:564-572; Panel B reproduced with permission from Mow VC, Proctor CS, Kelly

Musculoskeletal System, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA, Lea & Febiger, 1989, pp 31-57.)
Zone I: Superficial/Tangential
The superficial zone comprises the top 10% of tissue under the articular surface; in this zone,
collagen fibers are parallel to the articular surface, proteoglycan content is low, and water and
collagen contents are elevated.10,17
Supports cartilage surface lubrication and low-friction joint articulation1,18
Resists shear forces and minimizes stress to the other zones3,10
This zone has two distinct layers:
Lamina splendens: an acellular sheet with predominantly small collagen fibrils; this layer acts
as a barrier because no perichondrium is present.2
Cellular layer: with flattened chondrocytes aligned parallel to the articular surface2,19
Zone 2: Middle/Intermediate/Transitional
Constitutes 40% to 60% of cartilage thickness2,10
Characterized by random or oblique orientation of thick collagen fibers; large, rounded
chondrocytes; and increased proteoglycan content compared with the superficial layer1
o Provides resistance to cartilage compression3
Zone 3: Deep/Radial
Makes up approximately 30% of the articular cartilage2,10
In this zone, collagen fibers are thick and oriented perpendicular to the cartilage surface, and
chondrocytes appear as vertical clusters of rounded cells.8
The deep zone is characterized by high proteoglycan content and low cell density and water
content.1,10
Distributes loads and provides resistance primarily to compressive stress.3,4
Zone 4: Calcified
The calcified cartilage constitutes the boundary between the soft hyaline articular cartilage and
the underlying subchondral bone1,20 (Figure 5)

A thin basophilic line, called the tidemark, delineates the interface between the deep and
calcified zones, indicating the start of the calcified cartilage.2,10
This zone contains increased levels of calcium salts and hydroxyapatite crystals, and its
collagen fibers are radially oriented.1
Type X collagen produced by hypertrophic chondrocytes enhances anchorage with the
subchondral bone and mineralization of the ECM.8,11
The cement line separates calcified cartilage from subchondral bone.19
The subchondral bone consists of the subchondral bone plate (cortical bone), which is
directly below the calcified zone, and the subarticular spongiosa (trabecular bone), which
includes the trabeculae and other bony components.19,20
The spongiosa is vascularized with channels that penetrate the calcified zone from
below.19,21
With increasing age, bone gradually replaces cartilage, and the combined layers thin with
advancement of the tidemark.12,13
Figure 5 Schematic drawing shows the different layers of articular cartilage, the subchondral
bone plate, and the subarticular spongiosa. (Reproduced with permission from Madry H, van Dijk
CN, Mueller-Gerbl M: The basic science of the subchondral bone. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol
Arthrosc 2010;18[4]:419-433.)

Extracellular Matrix
The ECM is divided into three areas: the pericellular, territorial, and interterritorial matrices6,10
(Figure 6).
Pericellular matrix
Within the lacunae, closest to and surrounding the chondrocytes6
Thin layer rich in proteoglycans and noncollagenous proteins, lacking in collagen fibrils but
containing nonfibrillar type VI collagen11,22
Territorial matrix
Surrounds the lacunae, envelops the pericellular matrix, and is present throughout the
articular cartilage2,6
Thin layer composed of collagen fibrils that may extend to encompass two or more
chondrocytes1,22
Interterritorial matrix
The largest region, comprising everything outside the territorial matrix; this matrix
contributes to the mechanical properties of articular cartilage1,11
Contains mostly type II collagen (75%) and proteoglycans (22%)10,22
Figure 6 Schematic shows articular cartilage matrix regions. The three matrix regions depicted
with increasing distance from the chondrocyte are, respectively, pericellular, territorial, and
interterritorial. The matrix regions are present in all zones but are depicted in only one area in
the schematic. (Adapted with permission from Henry SE, Deasy BM, Chu CR: Articular cartilage:

Biology, biomechanics, and healing response, in Scott WN: Insall & Scott: Surgery of the Knee, ed 5.
Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2012, pp 146-152.)
Metabolism
Cellular Metabolism
Chondrocytes
Chondrocytes are responsible for metabolism and homeostasis.
Chondrocytes synthesize and build components of cartilaginous matrix and direct their
distribution within tissues.
Chondrocyte products include matrix proteins and GAG chains, which are secreted into the
ECM.
Chondrocyte metabolism is strongly influenced by the local environment.
Articular cartilage, dissimilar from most tissues, lacks vascular, lymphatic, and nerve supplies.
Cartilage exists in a hypoxic state, and oxygen levels within cartilage decrease with tissue
depth.
Cartilage relies on the diffusion of nutrients through the matrix from the surrounding
synovial fluid, subchondral bone, and chondrocytes.
Chondrocyte energy is obtained primarily via anaerobic glycolysis.
Extracellular Metabolism
Water
Water flow through the cartilage helps transport and distribute nutrients to chondrocytes.
Collagen
Collagen synthesis (Figure 7)
Knowledge about collagen synthesis has come primarily from studies of major fibrillar types
(ie, types I through III).
Hydroxylation requires vitamin C; a deficiency in this vitamin may alter collagen synthesis (eg,
causing scurvy).
Collagen catabolism
The mechanism is not completely understood.

In normal cartilage, the rate of breakdown is slow.
In degenerative cartilage and cartilage undergoing repair (eg, during skeletal growth),
breakdown and turnover are accelerated.
Enzymatic processes, such as the cleaving of the triple helix by metalloproteinases, have
been proposed.
Figure 7 Chart shows the events involved in the synthesis of collagen, along with the intracellular
site at which each step occurs. (Reproduced with permission from Mankin HJ, Brandt KD:
Biochemistry and metabolism of articular cartilage in osteoarthritis, in Moskowitz RW, Howell DS,
Goldberg VM, et al, eds: Osteoarthritis: Diagnosis and Medical/Surgical Management, ed 2.
Philadelphia, PA, WB Saunders, 1992, pp 109-154.)
Proteoglycans
Proteoglycan synthesis (Figure 8)
Proteoglycan assembly begins at the molecular level with gene expression, messenger RNA
transcription, translation, and aggregate formation.
The final molecule is formed with the addition of GAG and other posttranslational
modifications.

Figure 8 Illustration shows the various stages involved in the synthesis and secretion of
aggrecan and link protein by a chondrocyte. (1) The transcription of the aggrecan and link
protein genes to messenger RNA (mRNA). (2) The translation of the mRNA in the rough
endoplasmic reticulum (RER) to form the protein core of the aggrecan. (3) The newly formed
protein is transported from the RER to the (4) cis-and (5) medial trans-Golgi compartments,
where the glycosaminoglycan chains are added to the protein core. (6) On completion of the
glycosylation and sulfation, the molecules are transported via secretory vesicles to the plasma
membrane, where (7) they are released into the extracellular matrix. (8) Hyaluronate is
synthesized separately at the plasma membrane. (9) Only in the extracellular matrix can
aggrecan, link protein, and hyaluronate come together to form proteoglycan aggregates.
(Reproduced from Mankin HJ, Mow VC, Buckwalter JA, Iannotti JP, Ratcliffe A: Articular cartilage
structure, composition, and function, in Buckwalter JA, Einhorn TA, Simon SR, eds: Orthopaedic
Basic Science: Biology and Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System, ed 2. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2000, p 452.)
Proteoglycan catabolism (Figure 9)
Proteoglycans are continually broken down, even in the maintenance phase of cartilage.
Breakdown of proteoglycans is accelerated during degenerative processes, such as aging and
osteoarthritis.
Catabolism may be affected by the cellular signaling molecule interleukin (IL)-1 and joint
loading.

cartilage. The major proteolytic cleavage site is between the G1 and G2 domains, making the
glycosaminoglycan-containing portion of the aggrecan molecule nonaggregating. This fragment
can now be released from the cartilage. Other proteolytic events also can cause the G1 domain

Buckwalter JA, Iannotti JP, Ratcliffe A: Articular cartilage structure, composition, and function, in

the Musculoskeletal System, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2000, p 454.)
Growth Factors
Various growth factors and polypeptides are responsible for the regulation of cartilage
metabolism.
Platelet-derived growth factor 
In patients with osteoarthritis, platelet-derived growth factors may play an increased role in
healing.
Fibroblast growth factor-2 
Decreases proteoglycan synthesis 
Decreases aggrecanase activity
Upregulates MMPs
Transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)
TGF-β1 potentiates DNA synthesis and increases ECM synthesis and production.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:23 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage and Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002101
15/25

TGF-β1 prevents the degradative action of plasmin and stromelysins by stimulating the
formation of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase.
TGF-β1 also suppresses type II collagen synthesis.
In addition, TGF-β1 decreases the catabolic activity of IL-1 and MMPs.
Insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-I and IGF-II
IGF-I stimulates DNA and matrix synthesis in immature and adult articular cartilage; if
combined with TGF-β1, the effects are additive.
IGF-I decreases matrix catabolism, except in aged and osteoarthritic cartilage.
Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)-2 
BMP-2 stimulates ECM synthesis.
It also may partially reverse dedifferentiated phenotype in osteoarthritis by potently inducing
osteoblast differentiation in various cell types.
BMP-7/osteogenic protein-1 (OP-1)
BMP-7/OP-1 potentiates chondrogenic differentiation, with TGF-β increasing ECM synthesis.
BMP-7/OP-1 also decreases the catabolic activity of numerous cytokines, including IL-1 and
MMPs.
The activity of BMP-7/OP-1 is not affected by age or osteoarthritis.
Degradation
Breakdown
In normal metabolism, the cartilage matrix is broken down by the action of proteolytic
enzymes (ie, proteinases).
The primary proteinases involved in cartilage breakdown are the metalloproteinases
(collagenase, gelatinase, and stromelysin).
Overactivity of proteinases may play a role in the pathogenesis of osteoarthritis.
Metalloproteinases
The metalloproteinases include collagenase, gelatinase, and stromelysin.
Collagenase degrades native helical collagen fibrils.
Gelatinase degrades denatured type II and type IV collagen.
Stromelysin degrades the core of aggrecan.
Before activation, the metalloproteinases are synthesized as latent enzymes (proenzymes)
via enzymatic action.

Active enzymes can be inhibited irreversibly by tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase. The
ratio between metalloproteinases and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase determines
whether net metalloproteinase activity occurs.
Aging and Articular Cartilage
Immature Articular Cartilage
Immature and mature articular cartilages vary considerably (Table 1).
In the articular cartilage, age-associated changes include hypocellularity and zonal changes in
the distribution of chondrocytes, such as a decrease in the number of chondrocytes in the
superficial region and an increase in the number of cells in the deep layers.
With aging, chondrocytes may become less responsive to the proliferative effects of growth
factors, which may contribute to an imbalance in metabolic activity.
With age, chondrocytes also may grow larger, acquire increased lysosomal enzymes, and stop
dividing.
Mature Articular Cartilage
With aging and osteoarthritis, the amount and composition of the ECM in articular cartilage
changes.
Proteoglycan mass and size and concentrations of chondroitin sulfate decrease with aging,;
however, concentrations of keratan sulfate increase.
Protein content increases with aging, whereas water content decreases.
With age, cartilage loses its elasticity and becomes increasingly stiff; in addition, hydration of
the matrix and lubrication at its surface decrease.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
Mechanisms That Affect Cartilage Injury and Repair
Extracellular Matrix
Hyaline articular cartilage, which is avascular and aneural, is composed of chondrocytes and
extracellular water, collagen, and proteoglycans.
This cartilage has low metabolic activity with poor regenerative capacity.
In addition, articular cartilage is nourished by synovial fluid at the superficial zone and oxygen
diffusion from subchondral bone at the base, creating overall low oxygen tension. Therefore,
chondrocytes are primarily anaerobic.
Physiologic stress on a joint stimulates the synthesis of matrix products, whereas excess stress
may trigger chondrolysis and thinning.
Synovial Fluid
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:23 AM
AAOS | Articular Cartilage and Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002101
18/25

Preservation of the most superficial chondral layer, the lamina splendens, is critical for
protection of the deeper zones.
Synovial fluid lubricates the articular cartilage and provides nutrients to the superficial layer.
Synovial tissue is composed of two cell types: type A synoviocytes are involved in tissue
homeostasis and phagocytosis, whereas type B synoviocytes secrete synovial fluid.
Produces an ultrafiltrate of blood plasma that is secreted into the joint.
Synovial fluid is composed of hyaluronic acid, lubricin, prostaglandins, and MMPs.
Lubricin is the key lubricant of synovial fluid.
Synovial fluid has viscoelastic properties: it’s coefficient of friction increases with a lower shear
rate.
Synovium from arthritic or traumatized joints secretes high levels of inflammatory cytokines,
such as TNF-α and IL-1, which may directly degrade cartilage.
After joint trauma, the lubricin concentration and lubricating ability of synovial fluid are
impaired.
Lubrication 
Types of lubrication
Elastohydrodynamic: a form of hydrodynamic lubrication in which elastic deformation of the
contact surfaces supports a continuous fluid film; the primary form of lubrication during
dynamic joint movement (Figure 10).
Hydrodynamic: describes lubrication mechanisms involving a fluid film
Boundary: nondeformable bearing surfaces partially separated by a fluid film; superficial
zone proteins work via this method.
Boosted: fluid pools form between articulating surfaces, potentially increasing the coefficient
of friction between them.
Weeping: pressure on the superficial chondral zone can cause fluid shifts into the lubricating
layer.
Alterations in response to stress
The normal coefficient of friction of a joint is between 0.002 and 0.04.
The coefficient of friction is decreased with fluid film formation, elastic deformation of
articular cartilage, and synovial fluid.
Friction is directly increased by alteration of the chondral surface with fibrillation or gross
defects.

Chondral and Osteochondral Fractures
Epidemiology
Because many lesions are asymptomatic, the incidence and prevalence of these defects are
difficult to determine.
Evidence suggests that partial-thickness lesions may progress to full-thickness lesions, which
may initiate the onset of symptoms.
Microtrauma

Blunt impact or repetitive trauma may damage chondrocytes or cause microfracture of the
ECM. Although this trauma may not be grossly perceptible, it increases the rate of chondrocyte
apoptosis at the site of injury and the levels of degradative and inflammatory cytokines.
Chronic stress also may hasten thickening of the subchondral bone and thinning of the
chondral layer.
Superficial and Deep Lacerations
Superficial injuries that do not cross the tidemark generally do not heal. Because of limited
vascularity in this area, an inflammatory healing response cannot be initiated.
Chondrocyte apoptosis occurs rapidly at the margins of a wound. Although chondrocytes may
proliferate at the edges and local proteoglycan production increases, cells do not migrate into
or close the wound.
Because the defect remains open, the initial injury may propagate or enlarge with continued
joint loading. Even minor lesions alter hydrodynamic permeability, increasing force
transmission to the subchondral bone.
Deep injuries that cross the tidemark allow for the influx of blood products, which triggers a
triphasic inflammatory response.
Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells originating from the underlying bone marrow may
produce type I collagen, causing fibrocartilage to fill the site of injury.
Fibrocartilage has poor biomechanical properties compared with native hyaline cartilage.
Degenerative changes, including surface fibrillation, loss of matrix proteoglycans, and
chondrocyte death, may ensue.
Factors Affecting Repair
Various growth factors (eg, TGF-β, BMPs, IGF, fibroblast growth factor, and platelet-derived
growth factor) influence mesenchymal cell migration and differentiation into chondrocytes at
an injury site. Additional research is necessary to determine the ratio of cytokines, dose, and
delivery method required to stimulate the formation of hyaline cartilage after an injury (Figure
11).
Joint malalignment, meniscal insufficiency, and ligamentous instability (eg, anterior cruciate
ligament tear) increases focal contact pressures in the joint that may cause new chondral loss
or propagate existing loss.

Joint motion is critical for diffusion of nutrients to superficial chondral layers. Therefore,
continuous passive motion is believed to be beneficial to cartilage health and healing.
Conversely, joint immobilization leads to thinning, softening, and loss of proteoglycans from
the ECM.
